In-Depth Bulk Solids Engineering: Rizk Equation & Pressure Drop Models

In dilute-phase pneumatic conveying, particles are fully suspended in an airstream where gas drag balances gravity. If gas velocity drops below the critical saltation velocity ($u_s$), particles settle to the bottom of the horizontal pipe, forming rolling sand dunes that trigger pipeline blockage:

The Rizk Saltation Correlation

The universal industrial benchmark for horizontal saltation velocity is the empirical correlation established by Dr. F. Rizk (1973):

$$\mu = \frac{1}{\chi} \left( \frac{u_s}{\sqrt{g \, D}} \right)^{1/\delta} \left( \frac{D}{d_p} \right)^{\omega / \delta}$$
$$\text{Solving for } u_s: \quad u_s = \sqrt{g \, D} \times \left[ \chi \times \mu^\delta \times \left( \frac{d_p}{D} \right)^\omega \right]$$

Where:

  • $\mu$: Solid loading ratio (mass ratio of solids to conveying air: $\dot{m}_s / \dot{m}_{air}$). For dilute phase, typically $\mu \approx 3 - 15$.
  • $D$: Pipe internal diameter ($m$).
  • $d_p$: Mean particle diameter ($m$).
  • $\chi, \delta, \omega$: Dimensionless constants. For typical industrial granular and powdery solids: $\chi \approx 1100$, $\delta \approx 0.54$, $\omega \approx 0.10$.
  • $u_{design}$: Safe operating velocity: $u_{design} = (1.20 - 1.30) \times u_s$.

Two-Phase Pressure Drop Summation

The total pneumatic conveying pressure drop is decomposed into discrete physical resistances following the Barth / Weber / Marcus framework:

$$\Delta P_{total} = \Delta P_{gas} + \Delta P_{accel} + \Delta P_{solid\_fric} + \Delta P_{vert} + \Delta P_{bends}$$
$$\Delta P_{gas} = \lambda_g \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho_{air} u_g^2}{2}, \quad \Delta P_{accel} = \mu \, \rho_{air} \, u_g \, c_s$$
$$\Delta P_{solid\_fric} = \lambda_s \, \mu \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho_{air} u_g^2}{2}, \quad \Delta P_{vert} = \mu \, \rho_{air} \, g \, H_{vert}$$
$$\Delta P_{bends} = N_{bends} \times B \times \frac{\rho_{air} u_g^2}{2} (1 + \mu)$$

5 Fatal Engineering Pitfalls in Pneumatic Conveying Systems

1. Saltation Dune Collapse & Catastrophic Pipe Line Plugging

Operating below saltation velocity ($u_g < u_s$) causes particles to drop out of suspension and accumulate in dunes along horizontal pipe inverts. As the dune builds, cross-sectional area restricts, causing a sudden spike in pressure drop. If the positive-displacement Roots blower relief valve pops, all airflow stops, permanently packing hundreds of feet of pipe solid with compressed product.

2. Angel Hair & Snake Skin Generation in Polymer Pellet Transport

When conveying plastic pellets (polyethylene, polypropylene) at excessive velocities ($> 22 \text{ m/s}$), high-speed frictional heating melts pellet surfaces against smooth pipe walls. This leaves molten plastic ribbons called "angel hair" or "snake skins" that clog diverter valves, foul silo rotary airlocks, and contaminate injection molding lines. Mitigation requires shot-peened or spiral-grooved pipe surfaces and strict velocity throttling.

3. Pipe Elbow Abrasive Wear-Through & Blast Erosion

Abrasive particles (silica sand, alumina, cement) impact the outer radius of 90° pipe bends with kinetic energy proportional to velocity cubed ($E \propto u^3$). Standard schedule 40 steel elbows erode and blow out in less than 72 hours under high velocities. Industrial abrasive conveying demands induction-hardened pipe, ceramic-tiled elbows, or vortex pocket "blind tee" bends that form protective stationary material cushions.

4. Rotary Airlock Valve High-Pressure Blowback Gas Leakage

In positive-pressure systems, the rotary valve feeds solids from an atmospheric hopper into a 0.5–1.0 bar conveying line. Air leaks backward through rotor tip clearances. This upward "blowback air" fluidizes product in the feeding hopper throat, bridging material and cutting solid feed rate by up to 80%. A dedicated blowback venting shroud with dust collector return is mandatory.

5. Electrostatic Spark Discharge & Combustible Dust Deflagration

High-speed particulate conveying generates intense triboelectric static charges exceeding 30,000 volts. If any pipe spool, flex sleeve, or receiver cyclone lacks metallic bonding straps across flanges, static discharge sparks jump across gaps. In organic dust environments (sugar, flour, starch, plastic fines), this spark immediately ignites a catastrophic combustible dust explosion violating NFPA 652/654 standards.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is saltation velocity and why does it dictate dilute-phase pneumatic conveying? +
Saltation velocity (u_s) is the minimum superficial air velocity in a horizontal pipeline below which suspended solid particles drop out of the gas stream and settle onto the bottom pipe invert. Operating below saltation velocity triggers dune formation, slugging, severe pressure surges, and total pipe line blockage. Industrial dilute-phase systems are designed with an operating air velocity 20% to 30% above the Rizk saltation threshold.
How does the Rizk equation compute the saltation velocity? +
The Rizk correlation models the saltation Froude number (Fr_s = u_s / sqrt(g*D)) as an empirical function of solid loading mass ratio (μ = m_solids / m_air) and the ratio of particle diameter to pipe diameter (dp/D): Fr_s = [χ * μ^δ * (dp/D)^ω], where χ ≈ 1100, δ ≈ 0.54, and ω ≈ 0.10. Solving for u_s yields the exact velocity threshold for stable particle entrainment.
What is the Solid Loading Ratio (μ) and what are typical industrial values? +
The solid loading ratio (μ) is the dimensionless mass ratio of conveyed solids to conveying air: μ = mass flow rate of solids / mass flow rate of air (kg solids per kg air). In dilute-phase pneumatic conveying, μ typically ranges between 3 and 15 kg/kg. In dense-phase slug or plug flow systems, μ exceeds 30 to 100+ kg/kg.
Why do 90° pipe bends produce disproportionate pressure drop and abrasive wear? +
When high-speed particles enter a 90° elbow, centrifugal force drives them to the outer pipe radius where they decelerate through frictional impact and sliding against the wall. Upon exiting the bend, the gas stream must re-accelerate the solids back to transport velocity, consuming significant pressure energy. Abrasive materials (sand, fly ash) severely scour pipe walls; elbow wear rate increases exponentially with air velocity (Wear ∝ u^2.5 to u^3.5).
How is air expansion handled in long-distance pneumatic conveying pipelines? +
As air travels along the pipeline, friction causes pressure to drop. By Boyle's Law (P1*V1 = P2*V2), the gas expands, increasing volumetric flow and causing superficial air velocity to accelerate toward the discharge end. In long pipelines, this velocity rise can cause excessive pipe erosion and pellet degradation. Engineers prevent this by using 'stepped pipelines'—progressively increasing pipe diameter (e.g. from 100mm to 125mm to 150mm) to maintain air velocity within an optimal window.
